seoTitle: How to Add Wise to Stripe for Payouts (2026 Guide)
metaDescription: Connect a Wise multi-currency account to Stripe so you can receive payouts without a local bank account. Covers the exact dashboard path, the confirmation email rule most guides get backwards, and what to check first.
intro: Stripe pays out to a bank account in your own country by default, which is a problem the moment you don't have one. That's the normal situation for freelancers, remote agencies, and small international sellers. Wise's multi-currency account solves it by giving you local account details in several currencies, and Stripe will send payouts to it once the account is added and confirmed. The part that trips people up isn't finding the field to paste an account number. It's getting through Stripe's confirmation steps correctly, since one of them works the opposite way most people assume. This guide covers what Stripe checks before it accepts a new payout destination, the verification prompts you'll run into, and what changes once Wise is confirmed as your payout account.
prerequisites: A Stripe account with no unresolved requirements banner blocking payouts
A Wise account with a balance already opened in the currency you want Stripe paying out in
costNote: Stripe doesn't charge to add or change a payout destination. Opening a Wise account is free; Wise's own conversion fee applies only if you convert or spend the balance across currencies, not to the act of receiving a Stripe payout into it.

steps.heading: Why route Stripe payouts through Wise
steps.body: Stripe supports payouts to local bank accounts in a long list of countries, but not every country, and even where it's supported the currency options can be limited. Wise gets around this by issuing local receiving details tied to one account: a UK sort code and account number, a US routing number, a Eurozone IBAN, and more. Freelancers billing international clients and small businesses without a Stripe-supported home bank use this to receive payouts reliably, then hold the balance in whichever currency makes sense before converting it. Stripe explicitly supports paying out to accounts like this. You still have to clear Stripe's own verification steps before the new destination goes live.

steps.heading: Check that your Stripe account can pay out
steps.body: Before touching payout settings, open your Stripe dashboard and look for any banner about paused payments or payouts. A fresh or partially verified account often shows one at the top of the Home screen, above the balance summary. Stripe won't send anything anywhere, Wise included, until whatever it's asking for is resolved, so clear that first instead of discovering it mid-setup. The same Home screen is where you'll find your API keys and the rest of the navigation, so it's a reasonable first stop before you go looking for payout settings specifically.

image.caption: The Stripe dashboard Home screen, flagging that payments and payouts are paused until account requirements are met — worth resolving before adding a new payout destination.

steps.heading: Add your Wise details as a payout bank account
steps.body: Payout bank accounts live under Settings (the gear icon), then Business, then the Bank accounts and currencies tab. Adding one asks for the account holder name, the account number, and the routing number, or their local equivalents (sort code, IBAN) depending on the account's country. This is exactly the information your Wise account gives you once you've opened a balance in the matching currency, so keep the Wise dashboard open in another tab while you fill the form in. If your Stripe account handles more than one currency, each one needs its own bank account, and the currency on the account you add has to match the currency you want paid out. Only a user with Admin or Owner access on the Stripe account can add or edit bank details.

steps.heading: Confirm the change from your email
steps.body: Changing a payout destination is sensitive, so Stripe doesn't apply it immediately. It emails a verification link to the address on your account and asks you to leave the original tab open. Here's the part worth getting right: Stripe's own instructions say to click that link on the same device and same browser as the tab you started from, not a different one. The link is single-use and expires ten minutes after Stripe sends it. Click it from your phone while the request came from your laptop, or let it sit past the window, and you'll land on a "We couldn't verify your identity" error and have to request a fresh one.

image.caption: Stripe's email confirmation prompt after submitting a new payout destination. Click the link on the same device and browser as the tab that requested it, within ten minutes.

steps.heading: Clear a two-factor prompt if Stripe shows one
steps.body: Depending on your account's security settings, Stripe may also ask for a code from your authenticator app, or simply your password, before it finalizes the change. Not every account sees the same prompt here; it depends on what two-factor setup you already have enabled. Have your authenticator app open before you start the process regardless, since you don't want to be hunting for a code with a short expiry window while the confirmation email sits waiting.

image.caption: A two-factor verification prompt asking for a six-digit authenticator code, shown on accounts with two-factor authentication enabled.

steps.heading: What changes once Wise is verified
steps.body: Once the new account clears both checks, it appears in your payout settings as an active destination, and your Stripe balance starts routing there on whatever schedule you've set: daily, weekly, or monthly. From that point it behaves like any other connected bank account. Stripe pushes funds automatically, and you collect them in Wise, where you can hold, convert, or spend the balance across currencies instead of it landing in a single local account. Send yourself a small test payout the first time, or watch the next scheduled one closely, before relying on the setup for real client payments.

troubleshooting.problem: The confirmation link says "We couldn't verify your identity"
troubleshooting.cause: The link was opened on a different device or browser than the tab that requested the change, it was clicked more than once, or more than ten minutes passed after Stripe sent it.
troubleshooting.fix: Go back to the original tab and request a new confirmation email, then click the fresh link on that same device and browser within ten minutes. It won't work in a private or incognito window.

troubleshooting.problem: Stripe rejects the new bank account outright
troubleshooting.cause: The account's currency doesn't match the currency you're trying to pay out in, or the account details don't match what's on the Wise balance exactly.
troubleshooting.fix: Open a Wise balance in the currency you want, and copy the account number and routing details from that specific balance, not a different one.

troubleshooting.problem: The account sits unverified after adding it
troubleshooting.cause: Stripe sometimes needs to confirm a new bank account with two small deposits before it will pay out to it.
troubleshooting.fix: Watch for a Dashboard notification once the microdeposits land in Wise (usually within one to two business days), then enter the two amounts to verify the account.

faq.question: Why use Wise instead of a normal bank account with Stripe?
faq.answer: Wise is useful when Stripe doesn't support a bank account in your country, or when you want payouts in multiple currencies without a conversion fee every time money lands.

faq.question: Do I open the confirmation email on my phone or my computer?
faq.answer: Whichever device you started the change on. Stripe requires the confirmation link to be opened on the same device and browser as the original tab, not a different one, and the link expires after ten minutes.

faq.question: Will Stripe always ask for a two-factor code when I add Wise?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. It depends on the two-factor setup already on your account. The email confirmation step applies more consistently; the authenticator prompt shows up for accounts that have two-factor enabled.

faq.question: Can freelancers and international sellers use this setup?
faq.answer: Yes. It's aimed specifically at freelancers and small international businesses that don't have a Stripe-supported local bank account to fall back on.

faq.question: Does adding Wise cost anything?
faq.answer: No. Stripe doesn't charge to add a payout destination, and opening a Wise account is free. Wise's own fees apply only when you convert or spend the balance, not when Stripe pays into it.

verifiedNote: Click path and screens come from a recorded walkthrough. Re-checked against Stripe's own support articles on adding a payout bank account and on email link verification, September 2026. That check corrected the confirmation-email step: Stripe requires the link to be opened on the same device and browser as the original tab within ten minutes, not a different device as this guide previously suggested, and it softened the two-factor step, which Stripe's docs don't describe as guaranteed on every account. Wise's own published material confirms the integration exists but does not publish its own step-by-step for the Stripe side, so the dashboard path and field names here follow Stripe's documentation.
